Recent investigations into neural networks' resilience against malicious input have primarily focused on developing quantitative metrics for measuring robustness. This research diverges from this approach by scientifically explaining and quantifying adversarial example existence in neural networks using a specific architecture. Our study reveals that Neural ODEs possess inherent resistance to malintentioned data due to their nature as continuous functions. This inherent immunity is further substantiated by numerical and empirical analyses. In addition, our findings indicate that Neural ODEs' continuous domain may be the primary factor contributing to their enhanced robustness. This phenomenon is more pronounced in higher-dimensional spaces. Consequently, it is our belief that future research in measuring neural network robustness should prioritize qualitative analysis over quantitative assessment.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through the convolution of a given kernel and a solution, extensively applied to model vehicular traffic, have a singular local limit that has been extensively studied. This singular limit is about nonlocal solutions converging to the entropy-admissible solution of a classical conservation law with a point source, essentially replacing the convolution kernel with a delta function. In recent counter-examples it was shown that this singular limit doesn't necessarily converge for all cases, yet some specific results were proven for traffic models using anisotropic kernels under stringent assumptions, like an exponential decrease of kernels for certain variables. In our recent paper we've obtained general results of convergence for traffic models under less stringent assumptions than before, involving the use of anisotropic kernels with tailored behavior at their origins, illustrated by two new counter-examples showing that these assumptions are necessary. In this talk we'll discuss the main outcomes of our research.

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow transition maps of varying scale within their atlases, whereas translation surfaces remain at a fixed size. This results in dilation surfaces having directional flows with unique accumulation points, known as hyperbolic closed orbits that emerge from their induced nontrivial scaling effects. A hypothesis suggests that dilation surfaces lacking these hyperbolic closed orbits are equivalent to translation surfaces. Under the assumption of the existence of specific structural components, known as horizon saddle connections, in dilation surfaces, it is shown that the hyperbolic closed orbits are found densely in the surface of a unit circle. It has been also demonstrated that the said components, along with their geometric and elastic properties, are non-existent in translation surfaces.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity network based on total correlation and demonstrated its potential to serve as a biomarker for brain alterations. Specifically, we employed Correlation Explanation to estimate total correlation and verified the reliability of its estimates. By applying Correlation Explanation to data from 68 subjects in the Human Connectome Project, we generated a whole brain connectivity network and investigated its properties. Our results identified highly connected hubs consisting of posterior inferior temporal lobe, parietal cortex, and anterior temporal lobe, with an emphasis on semantic processing areas. Furthermore, we demonstrated that damage to these hubs in patients with schizophrenia, as determined by statistical analysis, differs significantly from conventional pair-wise measures focused on fronto-temporal networks.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that link the Schrödinger wave functions, complex Hermite polynomials, 
and Bargmann space holomorphic functions. This work extends the theory to three 
key unitary isomorphisms that link the Schrödinger wave functions, Weyl phase-space 
monomials, and Bargmann space holomorphic functions in the classical context. 
Furthermore, it develops the relevant unitary isomorphisms for harmonic wave 
packets, Weyl phase-space polynomials, and Bargmann space holomorphic polynomials. 
These results are viewed as providing mathematical justification for 
wave-particle duality.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and actionable predictions, incorporating sampling efficiency into their strategy. Traditional techniques are capable of handling standard Galerkin formulations but struggle with more advanced variants. This paper argues that conventional Monte Carlo methods have limitations when framing Gaussian process posterior distributions in a practical light and introduces a novel Monte Carlo approach as an intermediate solution. This approach converts the challenging task of navigating a curved Gaussian distribution into a simpler approximation involving approximately normally distributed per-dimensional components. A detailed evaluation demonstrates that this method surpasses random Monte Carlo approximations in precision and maintains efficiency; moreover, it lays the groundwork for integrating the proposed method into deep learning frameworks, paving the way for large-scale Gaussian process modeling.

This research demonstrates that in outdoor settings with wireless communications employing the IEEE 802.11 protocol using dipole antennas, ground reflection is a dominant signal propagation factor. Consequently, the Two-Ray model effectively forecasts signal strength with a satisfactory degree of accuracy for this environment. Notably, the study's findings are pertinent to UAVs-over-ground sensor communication, which entails these aerial vehicles gathering information collected by ground-positioned sensors while sustaining connectivity to the base station, thereby maintaining quality of service during their movement within the area.

The last ten years have been marked by significant breakthroughs in neutrino physics. Notably, multiple studies have conclusively proven the occurrence of neutrino flavor oscillations. We have established the parameters for neutrino mixing, which allows us to design more effective investigations of newly opened avenues of research. By taking precise measurements, we can test our current understanding of three types of neutrinos, their mass relationships, and CP symmetry in the lepton sector. Long-range neutrino experiments are expected to play a crucial role in enhancing our understanding of electroweak forces. The DUNE experiment, set up to capture the largest signal available, will play a key part in exploring CP symmetry, mass hierarchy, and deep learning applications using neutrino research. Our study presents the current DUNE physics objectives, the features of its detector design, its planned operation, and the anticipated results based on the data it will collect. We discuss how the LNV search potential of the DUNE experiment is also great. Furthermore, we discuss how the fact-finding capabilities of the DUNE experiment may be utilized.

A top quark, being the heaviest known elementary particle, serves as an optimal platform for exploring physics that goes beyond the standard model. The study of the associated bottom quark production in top pair events is particularly intriguing as it not only offers access to the fourth generation of fermions but also enables the examination of new physics in a broader context. This work focuses on examining the potential of measuring the associated bottom quark production in top pair events under the assumption of fourth generation existence. The study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically analyzing 300 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data. The investigation of associated bottom quark production in top pair events is realized by looking at two distinct signatures: a single top quark with two bottom quarks and two top quarks both accompanied by bottom quarks. The analysis leverages a novel method for identifying the associated bottom quark production in top pair events through a dedicated algorithm, known as TBW, utilizing bottom quark momentum reconstruction and an advanced kinematic analysis. The results of the study establish new physics reach for this specific process, thereby significantly enhancing the sensitivity to general new physics models, fourth generation couplings, and interactions with tbbq channels.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for Virtual Organizations formated as web services in the Semantic Web setting, focusing specifically on the Virtual Organization Virtual Service Component. The document also introduces the Virtual Organization Virtual Service Component as a generalization of web services that can encompass complex arrangements of services.  To facilitate understanding and management of such arrangements, the document introduces Virtual Organization Virtual Service Component abstractions, which enable refinement of unfulfilled requirements.  Moreover, the document provides definition keys for defining and comparing Virtual Organization Virtual service components, as well as a virtualization key for pairing suitable Virtual Organization virtual service components with available resources.  The document also includes a section explaining evaluation methods for determining client satisfaction during Virtual Organization virtual service delivery.  All definitions included in this document aim to improve the efficiency of Virtual Organization virtual service component management and processing during requirement refinement, deployment, operation, and requirement refinement processes.

To enhance the effectiveness of reinforcement learning through offline policy updating using experience replay, we need to address two key challenges. Firstly, standard offline replay relies on a well-formed dataset, but in practical scenarios, we often face suboptimal policies that don't work well for sampling. Secondly, even when a more suitable policy is used, the non-stationary nature of some reinforcement learning problems means that a reusable dataset can't be effectively used across different samples. To overcome these obstacles, we propose the Temporal Variance Reduction Policy (TVP) that exploits temporal correlations in rewards and uses variational learning to improve policies when faced with both stationary and non-stationary environments. In contrast to previous approaches, TVP successfully handles low-data scenarios, suboptimal policies, and non-stationary environments. Moreover, we find that TVP shares similarities with QMIX, a well-known method, but while QMIX assumes a specific structure for the mean-field assumption, TVP takes a more flexible approach by learning this structure directly through variational learning. When tested on a range of scenarios, TVP achieved superior results compared to other methods.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization technique serve to introduce supersymmetric variables that facilitate this extension. Though the strategies offer alternative approaches to achieving this goal, they haven't been extensively explored in relation to specific matrix ensembles. Notably, the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation strategy has seen earlier application in this context. The primary focus of this review is to introduce the superbosonization technique and its specific usage in deriving supersymmetric integrals for rotation-invariant matrices such as circular and spherical matrices. Additionally, the review examines recent extensions to gamma-distributed and lognormal matrices using the superbosonization technique.

This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning approach, known as ST-PL, that uses short observed sequences to predict future times and locations. The current implementation of ST-PL consists of a PL network that outputs a combined forecast. However, this method has difficulties including various plausible future forecasts in the overall forecast, leading to poor performance when there are multiple likely destinations. To overcome these challenges, this research introduces a new forecasting technique called Bi-ST-PL, separating the prediction process into two distinct PL networks that output separate future forecast distributions. The first PL network predicts the likelihood of future locations, and the second PL predicts the probability distribution of time while utilizing the first network's output to estimate the future location distribution. This allows the PL networks to share low-level features and convey more detailed information about locations. The accuracy of Bi-ST-PL was tested using the Stanford MobileRobot Dataset, demonstrating that it surpasses the performance of standard ST-PL, features a more continuous and consistent location forecast, and produces a structured distribution of possible locations, making it useful for tasks that require predicting a series of locations.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing safety concepts for linear capabilities to languages with lazy memory management, incorporating a range of fundamental control structures. This initial analysis is preliminary, aiming to integrate the benefits of garbage collection with advanced type systems.

Theoretical particles called heavy neutral leptons have the potential to resolve long-standing problems in physics, particularly those related to neutrino oscillations. These particles, being unable to interact with the standard model in the same way as other matter particles, have such properties that they avoid being constrained by experiments. However, the particles can still interact with leptons in the standard model through a specific interaction called the Z boson. Researchers have proposed that this interaction can be observed by looking at the missing energy signal in the collision of a hadron beam and an electron beam. The current experimental limits on this interaction can be exceeded by reaching energies of over a GeV. The particles can also interact through the Higgs boson. Researchers estimate that this interaction would result in a specific pattern of decay products that could be identified through experimental analysis.

Permutation decoding has become more prominent lately, particularly for polar codes, due to its ability to utilize a wide range of cyclic redundancy check codes. The decoding algorithm involves trying different permutations until the received vector matches the transmitted vector, with the success of permutation decoding depending on the diversity order. This paper examines permutation decoding for polar codes, focusing on its diversity order and decoding failure probability bounds. The analysis is then applied to a specific scenario involving polar codes over binary memoryless channels. The results show that permutation decoding can offer superior performance, particularly when the channel is well-conditioned, at a decoding cost comparable to standard CRC-based methods. However, the decoding efficiency drops rapidly as the channel becomes poorer, making its performance advantages less noticeable. The analysis also provides a way to calculate the decoding failure probability and diversity order for any given permutation decoding error rate.

We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves investigating under what conditions co-adding linearly acquired images yields an image with a defined point spread function. Our investigation spans co-adding methods applicable to both uniform and non-uniform exposure patterns. A comprehensive examination of the inherent characteristics of nonlinear image processing techniques also follows. Ultimately, two fundamental limitations define the point spread function of linear co-adding techniques, whereas we show that nonlinear co-adding can circumvent these restrictions entirely. Our conclusions indicate that current nonlinear co-adding methods, such as their advanced variants, fail to meet even one of the two critical conditions necessary for an image with a defined point spread function to be considered "well-defined." Consequently, all such images fall short of meeting even a moderately stringent requirement for an image to be considered "well-defined."

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that in perfect, undamaged crystals, there is a inherent weakness due to the presence of dislocations. It is then assumed that these dislocations remain in equilibrium states that are stable from a thermodynamic perspective. It is demonstrated that the line tension of a dislocation governs its movement in response to external pressures and the presence of other dislocations. Critical analysis of the governing forces and interactions leads to the conclusion that dislocations can only be moved by the solid when it is under specific geometric and mechanical conditions, such as notches or points of tri-axial stress. Furthermore, it is argued that the fracture process in crystals is a gradual one, brought about by the movement of dislocations. It is also proposed that the fracture threshold of a solid can be characterized by the presence of minimal surface irregularities on its structure. These irregularities can be thought of as small stress concentrations that facilitate dislocation movement and subsequently, fracture.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made through both the action of the Lie group SL(2,ℝ) and the Lie group SL(ℝ^2) via their respective automorphisms, effective field theories, and the Dyson model.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a less computationally powerful classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The fastest known protocol for verifying classical results in quantum computation has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|^3) and was published in 2021, however, this protocol's efficiency could be significantly improved to O(poly(κ)|C|) if quantum acceleration can be applied, where κ represents the quantum speedup benefit and |C| is the number of qubits in the quantum circuit. A more recent, multi-server protocol uses asymptotically fewer steps and can verify classical results much faster, at O(poly(κ)|C|) in both single-qubit and multi-qubit computations.

A blockchain system has been recognized as a potential solution for several Internet of Things (IoT) issues, including security, data storage, and transaction verification. However, the incorporation of blockchain in IoT applications is hindered by high computational and energy consumption rates, which are largely caused by the need for nodes to solve complex cryptographic puzzles. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel blockchain architecture called Li-Block, which leverages lightweight consensus and employs a lightweight cryptographic technique to ensure transaction validity through node polling. Theoretical performance assessments and simulations have been conducted to validate the efficiency of our proposed design.

A novel neural network approach for cell shape analysis, termed CellNet, uses signed distance functions to represent cell contours through level sets of signed distance maps, offering advantages over voxel-based and polygon mesh representations. This method can learn cellular geometry with any level of detail, accurately capturing characteristics not based on mesh topology and allowing for robust analysis of shapes. CellNet's ability to predict probabilities and quantities at any point in 3D space makes it suitable for various downstream tasks. In comprehensive benchmarking experiments, neural networks trained with SDFs outperformed those trained with voxel and mesh representations, demonstrating robustness and generalization under different conditions. CellNet outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in identifying growth patterns of lung adenocarcinoma from 4D CT scans, including predicting cell type at any point, identifying bronchial walls, and quantifying the epithelial mesenchymal transition process. This method can be applied to various downstream tasks in computational biology, including contiguity analysis, morphological pattern recognition, and quantitative pathobiology.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as references, citations, and footnotes. Although existing access methods like braille or other alternatives do not effectively address reference accessibility, we propose a new approach. We begin by identifying key challenges in reference accessibility and outlining our framework for achieving meaningful access. Our framework comprises three core components: providing reference summaries, allowing direct access to individual references, and ensuring linearized reference presentation. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach through a prototype application.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, requiring large, carefully curated datasets, and being challenging to fine-tune for long-range contextual relationships. To address these limitations, we introduce XLNet, a novel language modeling approach extending BERT's method using autoregressive language modeling to prioritize sequential understanding. We enable this by leveraging permutations of text sequences followed by a masked language modeling objective. Experimentally, our method outperforms BERT in 20 out of 21 comprehensive tests, often by significant margins, and when compared to BERT variants pre-trained on much larger datasets, we achieve competitive results with a model roughly 70% smaller in parameters.

We've developed computational models aimed at assessing the influence of stellar activity on spectroscopic analysis of exoplanet transits, particularly focusing on atmospheric characterization, in systems with both low and high resolution spectroscopic data. We've analyzed models representing three archetypal planetary systems, including a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting a K-type star, a Neptune-sized planet surrounding an M-dwarf star, and terrestrial planets in orbit around an M-dwarf star, specifically TRAPPIST-1. We've integrated stellar models incorporating temperature and velocity data, and found that contamination, stellar effects such as the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect, and center-to-limb variations significantly impact transit spectra. We discovered that low-frequency variability typically causes large-scale features such as temperature inversions or hazes, while high-frequency variability can indicate water features or carbon/dust signatures. We found that, in systems involving cooler stars, stellar activity easily dominates, hiding planetary effects. We had optimistic and pessimistic scenarios of stellar activity which showed that, in systems involving earlier type stars, planetary effects might still be obscured by stellar variability after removing noise. We concluded that stellar activity could easily distort planetary effects making their detection success purely dependent on the characteristics of the host star.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-forms. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially established by Troyanov.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this species moves using waves in the opposite direction, from tail to head. It tends to sink when its movements cause water to move towards its head, and can also rise to the surface by creating waves that push water towards its tail. When swimming, the centipede lifts its most anterior legs off the surface, and moves primarily in the top layer of water, with some instances of it crawling on the surface of the water, or diving beneath for short periods of time. Observing this species at different depths reveals that it may use a combination of waves and movements of its body to create currents that help it move downwards towards its preferred habitat at deeper levels.

The ultimate aim of this project is the creation of highly detailed simulation tools that can accurately depict tsunami behavior that is affected by dispersal over long periods. Dispersive models are crucial in situations such as a massive Pacific Island being hit by a tsunami where the speed of the wave depends on its depth. Non-dispersive models that are often used in educational and emergency response situations cannot accurately predict the outcome of such an event. High-resolution simulations that incorporate dispersal and are run over a short period of time have been demonstrated to converge into the outcomes predicted by dispersive models. An overview of the underlying mathematical framework, the methodology, and the first prototype of the simulator will be presented, with a focus on its performance in a complex scenario: the simulated arrival of a tsunami in the Pacific Island area following an artificially generated wave with varying levels of dispersal.

Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large, distant galaxies that are too faint to be seen in UV imaging taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. These galaxies have been referred to as HST-dark due to their elusive nature. Using high-resolution near-infrared imaging taken by the NIRCam camera, we have observed and analyzed the characteristics of 33 of these galaxies. These galaxies have been found to be highly obscured by dust, very massive, and highly star-forming at redshifts of 2 to 8. This study has provided a more complete understanding of the distribution of large galaxies in the universe at very early stages of its formation, and it has been revealed that a significant portion of large galaxies have been missing from previous observations. These galaxies have been found to lie along large-scale structures of galaxies that stretch across more than 100,000 light-years in length. The study has also provided a new constraint that suggests large galaxies have accounted for less than one percent of the total amount of dust in the universe, and it has been found to be consistent with predictions made by a model that suggests large galaxies have emerged at a relatively late stage in the universe's formation.

By incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we form a novel seven-dimensional theory of gravity. Depending on specific constant values, these terms may be equivalent to a 3-form field equation correction in eleven-dimensional supergravity. The complete equations of motion are subsequently determined. Interestingly, the addition of these terms leaves static, spherically-symmetric black holes unchanged. The new theory also yields AdS_7 spaces, squashed seven-dimensional spheres, and Q^{111} spaces in a Euclidean signature.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure all the disks come into contact with one of the container's walls when in a jammed state, resulting from a combination of external forces such as moderate pressure, gravity, and random vibrations. By dividing the disk arrangement into segments and constructing species of particles with statistically interacting behaviors, exact calculations for jammed configurations are obtained, allowing for a detailed understanding of volume and entropy. These jammed configurations are found to depend on specific dimensionless control parameters, representing the balance between work applied against the pistons, gravitational potential, and intensity of external agitations. These control parameters dictate the configurational statistics and influence the disk arrangement, leading to distinct characteristics based on weight variations. This framework can potentially be extended to random disk sequences using a modified jamming protocol.

Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using linear models which assumes uniform statistical properties or applying multivariate analysis to detrended time-series in conjunction with statistical inference. In this study, we utilize a different approach by focusing on individual components of the flavioral Enso indices and applying non-linear multivariate analysis to better distinguish between ENSO's different flavors. Our results show that Central Pacific Enso has a more pronounced impact on a smaller set of variables than East Pacific Enso, highlighting the distinct statistical characteristics of each type. Our analysis yields detailed spatial precipitation maps which illustrate the differing impacts of the two main flavors on global seasonal precipitation patterns. Our results are further validated by examining the fluctuations in satellite measurements of cloud cover over Central Pacific during the periods of strong cloud-related Enso correlations.

When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to mechanical pressure, the distortion they undergo may deviate from expected behavior, even within their elastic range. The extent of nonaffine behavior, a concept observed in various numerical models, poses a significant challenge to experimental studies due to its low amplitude and localized nature. A new technique has been developed for analyzing this nonaffine contribution, involving compensating for waves scattered by a stretched, amorphous material using precision adjustments to the optical probe's wavelength. The successful application of this approach has been demonstrated in two disordered materials with different chemical compositions, where experimental results have shown consistency with theoretical predictions under specific conditions. The observed outcomes may have important implications for understanding how geometric properties influence the mechanical response of amorphous materials and disordered polymer fibers.

This research investigates a population model, factoring in the effects of age and environmental pollution, comprising a single population with distinct larval and adult stages. The model uses logistic functions, and larvae are converted into adults at a constant rate, focusing solely on adult development. A systematic analysis reveals the equilibrium points and types of bifurcations that occur in this system, including the emergence of a limit cycle. Specifically, we identify the conditions that lead to a stable limit cycle, and show how environmental pollution and population growth interact and affect the emergence of oscillations.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, specifically those with certain weakening and contraction properties. This achievement builds on a previous result regarding the contraction counterparts of these extensions, while the computational complexity was not determined for them. In this study, we introduce just the necessary concepts related to well-quasi-orderings and fast-growing complexity classes, allowing us to provide upper bounds of $2^{(\cdot)^{O(\log \log \cdot)}}$ for the time and space complexities of algorithmic decision-making in these extensions.

Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research has sought to automatically enhance taxonomies by learning concept representations in Euclidean space. However, the natural geometric structure of taxonomies aligns better with hyperbolic properties, making this space more suitable for representation. We propose HyperExpan, an algorithm that preserves the hierarchical structure of a taxonomy within a more expressive hyperbolic embedding space. It employs graph neural networks to capture relationships and combines it with existing methods of learning from text data. HyperExpan surpasses the performance of baseline models that utilize Euclidean space representation learning in addressing taxonomy expansion tasks.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the dipole electric properties of molecular dimers in the S66 dataset using a highly advanced theoretical framework, namely CCSD(T)-F12b/aug-cc-pVDZ-F12 as a reference. When the external electric field reaches up to approximately 5 GV m^-1, higher-order electric responses are negligible. However, when it comes to dimers held together by hydrogen bonding along the intermolecular axis, we observe substantial variations in dipole moments. On the other hand, dimers bonded via pi-stacking or London dispersion exhibit small changes in dipole moments. Calculations of interaction polarizabilities suggest a positive-valued principal component aligned with the intermolecular axis, alongside two negative-valued components. Furthermore, energy decomposition via SAPT0/jun-cc-pVDZ reveals that electrostatics play a pivotal role in the interaction dipole moment, establishing a quantifiable connection. An in-depth examination of the S66 dataset has shown that dimers governed by hydrogen bonding or pi-stacking exhibit interaction dipole moments primarily due to orientationally dependent induced dipole moments.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and efficiency, incorporating data analytics and cyber-physical systems for enhanced planning and scheduling. Nonetheless, uncertainties inherent in environmental factors and operator subjectivity often go unaccounted for in decision-making, causing shipment delays and inaccuracies in budget projections. This widespread issue demands correction, and existing approaches have explored solutions via stochastic or fuzzy logic models. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for quantifying non-deterministic uncertainty through probabilistic modeling, which is universally applicable to various industrial datasets. Its adaptability and use of epsilon-contamination for handling limited data sets are key strengths. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a real-world dataset in Flanders, Belgium, yielding quantifiable outcomes that can inform industrial decision-making and improve credibility.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. We provide a measurable Resilience Satisfaction Value, which evaluates resiliency on a scale, considering two key factors: swift recovery from disturbances and sustained stability. The practicality of our approach is demonstrated through the use of case studies, marking a breakthrough in understanding multi-dimensional resiliency semantics.

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details ongoing and future searches for dark matter particles such as feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, scalar domain walls, and axion quark nuggets, employing accelerometers in a network configuration and discusses how atomic interferometry-based networks might enhance these searches.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which have a positive, smooth, and bounded u. The equation u_t is given by \[ \Delta u - \nabla \phi \cdot \nabla u = (au + b) \log u. \] In our analysis, \phi is a twice continuously differentiable function and a and b are non-zero constants. Our findings extend existing work from Souplet and Zhang (2006) and Wu (2008).

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It shows that sources under 5 inches exhibit lower polarization than larger sources, indicating a maximum polarization threshold. Additionally, a correlation between radio luminosity and polarization was found, particularly for large sources, whereas a weaker correlation was observed between median fractional polarization and luminosity for small sources.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having an inaccessible internal state, which can still reveal information. HMMs can be graphically represented through three joint probability distributions. HMMs can represent the distribution of observed data, but in an indirect manner through the connection to hidden states. Decoding HMMs, which means finding the hidden states that are most likely to have caused a given set of data, is a fundamental problem and has proven challenging due to the typically high dimension of the hidden states. Most research seeks probabilistic approaches to decoding HMMs, which involve computing an exhaustive list of possible hidden states and their associated probabilities, but this can be computationally expensive. In this research, we employ a message passing framework, inspired by the nature of HMMs as probabilistic models, to facilitate decoding. We also extend the capabilities of HMMs to include models with branching hidden states, which can give rise to tree-like sequences of data. We validate our model by achieving an experimental average-time complexity of O(n) in cases where the hidden states are of a fixed dimension and the observed data sequence is of length n. We compare our model specifically with the Bayesian inference algorithm for HMMs, but our approach has broader applications to other types of Bayesian networks that have temporal dimensions to their parameters.

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process marking turbulence's distinct feature: lacking invariant states. We tackle the challenges posed by these stochastic problems using homogenization techniques for equations with stationary, periodic, and random coefficients. Our approach focuses on the periodic case, mediating between exact stochastic two-scale representations and a simplified stochastic homogenized equation through a uniformly Lipschitz corrector equation. We demonstrate the large-scale stochastic oscillations that dominate the behavior, as well as explicit computable estimates of the corresponding velocities and diffusion coefficients. Our work significantly simplifies the analysis and numerical computation by bridging the exact two-scale representations and a straightforward stochastic homogenized equation via a fundamental corrector equation.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
lacking a complete understanding of the dynamics behind nucleon-nucleus and
nucleus-nucleus scattering. When phenomenological models are too limited,
key information about the processes is lost. We advocate an alternative
phenomenology for nuclear elastic scattering involving nucleons and light nuclei,
which effectively evaluates folding models and leverages available empirical
evidence, particularly relevant for interactions involving nucleons and light ions.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation behavior in a thin conductor plate separated by two large vacuum areas at extremely low temperatures. The research demonstrates that the usual high-temperature behavior of the free energy, also known as the Helmholtz free energy, cannot be achieved at extremely low temperatures. Consequently, the model expands on the free energy for both high and low temperature scenarios, resulting in the anticipation of novel thermodynamic properties and phases at extremely low temperatures. Specifically, the research predicts the existence of two distinct phases at extremely low temperatures: a uniform and a uniform magnetic phase, with both phases potentially existing in equilibrium with each other. Additionally, the model accurately predicts previously observed thermal, magnetic, and electric properties, such as the existence of zero-energy thermal entropy, magnetic entropy and the expectation of a superconducting behavior rather than usual gas behavior at extremely low temperatures.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'{e}gion d'Inter\'{e}gration de L'H\'{i}stoire (RIHS) method deploys an Eulerian network to minimize the presumed knowledge an adversary might have about a user's sequence of locations. This adversary hypothesizes that locations shared within a short time frame have connections. Our approach reschedules a user's arrival times to minimize an adversary's ability to infer locations shared within a short time frame, while also preserving a predetermined level of privacy. Our method benefits from using an Eulerian network, which simplifies the process of scheduling arrival times to minimize an adversary's ability to infer locations shared within a short time frame. We now prove the optimal privacy that can be achieved, as well as provide an algorithm that can calculate this optimal value. Our method benefits from using an Eulerian network, which not only simplifies the mathematical calculations involved but also reduces the complexity of the algorithm and makes it more scalable. Our method deploys a distance metric that balances privacy and serviceability, which can be easily implemented using an Eulerian network but requires a more complex implementation when using an undirected graph with weighted edges.

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling real-time, large-scale place recognition using 3D point clouds. The methodology utilizes the 3D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation to summarize dense point clouds into geometrical shape descriptions via probabilistic distributions. Subsequently, the novel NDT-Transformer network processes a set of 3D NDT cell representations to learn global descriptors enriched with geometric context, ultimately enhancing both discriminative and generative characteristics. The described method demonstrates exceptional performance in a real-world evaluation, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the proposed implementation facilitates efficient processing on the GPU, thus enabling real-time performance even at large scales.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed functional networks are consistently present across all sites, and inter-site effects were relatively minor. Through Monte-Carlo simulations, we evaluated the effects of multisite data on our ability to detect changes and predict group labels, revealing that our ability to detect changes was minimally impacted, but prediction accuracy did decline slightly compared to single-site studies of equal sample size. Our results imply that large sample sizes can make multisite research in the brain feasible and efficient.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed text have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the NLP needs of languages that are spoken as a mix of two or more languages in various contexts. 
Given that languages like Hindi-Urdu and Modern Indian languages have no standard scripts, creating representative word embeddings poses a significant challenge. 
To overcome this, we have developed a novel approach that combines data augmentation with Neural Relational Embeddings, resulting in improved performance on tasks like fake account detection in Maltese-English code-mixed text, and named entity recognition in Hindi-English code-mixed text. 
Our method also allows for the direct application of this technique to tasks involving single language text, like fake account detection. 
To further facilitate development in this area, we are releasing heritable versions of the HCRN and CRN models, where the parent node can assume multiple forms, along with carefully designed datasets to help researchers démarrer their investigations.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experiments, particularly at high pressures, suggesting the importance of its van Hove singularities in superconducting H3S compounds.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are often unsuccessful without pre-compiled maps or where environmental maps become obsolete due to moving obstacles. A novel framework utilizes dynamic obstacle shapes to create ad-hoc spatial boundaries for navigation in unstructured environments. We develop a system to generate these shapes through the application of a dynamic occupancy map and filter out unrealistic scenarios. The resulting shapes are integrated into a probabilistic space, defining the validity of states in 2D and 3D space. We adapted the Tree-based Field-Field Interpolation method to calculate the trajectory by incorporating the validity shapes. Our approach was compared with other methods in terms of success rate and computational efficiency in both simulated and real-world scenarios. The results show that our technique achieves high performance and competitiveness when compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique that exploits dynamic scenes featuring moving objects by creating a three-dimensional surfel map. Our method aims to identify the target image's viewing direction and calculate its distance to the camera, which is then used to estimate the image's pose. By accounting for changes in object positions within the scene, our approach can tackle dynamic environments. Our method has been successfully tested on the KITTI dataset, which is commonly used for self-driving research. Unlike other techniques that assume a static environment, our method employs a probabilistic framework to track changes in object positions and maintains a surfel representation of 3D points, which are precision-improving features. By comparing our method to other techniques in both static and dynamic environments, our experiments demonstrate its superiority. Furthermore, our method's accuracy was also compared to that of other learning-based techniques, such as neural networks, with results indicating that a surfel-based approach can surpass neural networks in terms of accuracy.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the novel algorithm addresses two key challenges: minimizing the impact of hardware constraints and maximizing the spectral efficiency. By leveraging these modifications, the paper develops a dual solution, the group sparsity-based reconfiguring of ZF precoding, which can be formulated as a convex problem and yields significant improvements in spectral efficiency with reduced computational overhead compared to the maximum ratio precoding approach.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be generated by a finite set of rational functions over the semifield of the second curve, provided that the preimages of the Weil-Petersson ball B^4 are covered by a finite number of sets, that are defined over the semifield.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions.

We've demonstrated that combining the 31st Khovanov homology of a link's untwisted Heegaard-Fraese diagram with a Vassiliev invariant of order two yields a comprehensive link invariant that retains its properties for both its singular values and band sums. While this doesn't directly result in a comprehensive link invariant, it offers insight into the nature of the slice link invariant and serves as a scenario in which the combination of two Vassiliev invariants produces a stronger invariant. Furthermore, it is suggested that incorporating the slice link invariant into the combined invariant could overcome the limitation that usually arises from band sums.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most of these materials superconductivity develops out of a nematic antiferromagnetic state, the case of LiFeAs stands out with its high superconducting critical temperature and absence of magnetic ordering. Despite this distinction, it is widely accepted that the superconducting state of LiFeAs shares key similarities with its nematogenic counterparts. If this is indeed the case, it would require that the two states be closely linked by a continuous evolution triggered by external stress. Our study demonstrates that the application of uniaxial compression to LiFeAs results in a significant modification of its nematic symmetry characteristics, measured using x-ray linear dichroity in situ stress experiments. At 145 kPa, a substantial change occurs in the orientation of the symmetry axis, indicating that the antiferromagnetic nematic domain gives way to a stress-induced orthorhombic state. Importantly, our findings show that the superconducting state of LiFeAs does not exhibit stress-induced nematic behavior in contrast to its stress-induced nematic antiferromagnetic counterparts. As a result, this study rules out the possibility that stress induces superconductivity in LiFeAs through a means similar to that observed in other iron-based superconductors. Furthermore, it challenges the universality of the link between superconductivity and nematicity

This research reviews a global analysis of Type-II two Higgs doublet models and considers how upcoming measurements of the SM-like Higgs and Z-pole may influence allowed model parameters. Based on a global analysis of two Higgs doublet models using the GAMBIT tool, our study takes into account numerous current constraints, including theoretical requirements, experimental search results, and physical constraints on flavour. Furthermore, we evaluate whether forthcoming facilities, like the High-Luminosity LHC, the Circular Electron Positron Collider, the International Linear Collider, and the Future Circular Collider, electron edition will be capable of probing two Higgs doublet model parameters.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles and temporal strategies for enhancing spontaneous particle assembly. By directly optimizing a goal-based objective, our algorithm consistently produces particles which effectively bind to a specific surface at equilibrium, a phenomenon that has been previously designed via reverse engineering. Our results notably show that the parameter settings for these optimized particles do not require manual fine-tuning and exhibit a pronounced degree of chemical stability. We delve into the evolutionary dynamics of the optimized particles and explore how their design principles can be extrapolated to a variety of related challenges, providing a promising evolutionary solution to a fundamental problem in supramolecular chemistry, namely creating stable, assembled structures on irregular surfaces.

Our research involves studying the dynamical-Higgs-phase scenario in a class of chiral gauge theories that are strongly coupled. We concentrate on two specific theories: the massless $U(N)_1 \otimes U(N)_2$ chiral gauge theory with global $S_N$ symmetry and the minimally-damped $U(1)_L \otimes U(1)_R$ chiral gauge theory. In both cases, our analysis reveals that gauge boson condensation leads to a non-perturbative formation of Higgs vacuums. Furthermore, we investigate how symmetry-breaking dynamics of this type may apply to the strong flavor physics of the quarkyonic phase, which is present in QCD. Specifically, we show that while the Higgsed-photon scenario does not occur in QCD, the dynamical-Higgs scenario could potentially facilitate large-$N$ consistent resurgences of compositeness and chiral invariance that mimic some features of the near-conformal QCD.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between input force and resulting flow motion in a bounded space, and find that the equation remains well-suited for analysis in high dimensions when the input follows certain patterns. This leads to a series of functional analysis conclusions, specifically that a specific group of functions known as $Q}_{q,s}^{q}(\mathbb R^d)$ remains well-defined. This contributes towards the goal of proving the equation's stability for dimensions greater than two and specific wave patterns, and paves the way for potential applications in pattern recognition.

We are studying how the interactions between magnons impact the dispersion and
polarization of these magnons in specific types of magnetic insulators when
heated. By applying a certain approximation, we've been able to examine how the
interactions between these magnons change their behavior when the system is at
finite temperatures. Initially, we've found that in certain scenarios, the
interaction of opposite spins doesn't affect the magnon's band structure. We
then went on to investigate how the interaction of adjacent spins affects the
spin of these magnon modes. Under certain conditions, we found that the spin
polarization of these magnon modes becomes exchange-coupled multiple times. 
Furthermore, we've identified that in the case where the high-frequency modes
don't interact with each other, the low-frequency modes tend to be either
polarized in the spin or the spin, with the high-frequency modes tending to
be polarized in the spin. We observed this behavior in the specific type of material
when the spin tendency towards interaction is greater than the spin tendency,
which typically occurs in cases where the material has a certain type of spin
structure called a "stripe" and the magnetic fields are relatively small.

This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, specifically against linear algebra attacks. It commence's by examining how far subspaces can be taken using the generic group challenge procedure over the fields $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$ and $m=4,6,8,10,12$. It then details two secure choices for the parameter $k$, depending on the size of $m$. Finally, the study concludes with a detailed description of the secure parameter sets for $m \geq 4$.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and subsequently fine-tuned for specific tasks, our research introduces a
new method to guide the training of PLMs prior to application. The proposed
self-guided training (SeGT) approach has three key objectives: enhance the
representational robustness of PLMs against various text manipulations; boost
the fluency of generated text by reducing common mistakes associated with
PLMs; and optimize the ability of PLMs to generalize on new data by
consequently enhancing their performance in transfer and fine-tuning settings.
Three publicly accessible tools are provided for evaluation: (1) a text
manipulation dataset for testing robustness, (2) a paragraph modification
dataset for enhancing fluency, and (3) a vast dataset for transfer and
fine-tuning settings. Our findings demonstrate significant advancements in the
area of representation learning within PLMs.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular type of acyclic graphs called simple flag complexes. Recent studies focused on the latter revealed interesting asymptotic behavior in the weights of these structures. Here, we explore the same concept for the former by examining random geometric shapes in the plane, called Delaunay meshes, and their substructures, the alpha-shapes. We show that knowing only part of the mesh weights is enough to yield a statistically significant result about their distribution, providing a useful alternative to the earlier mentioned structures. Our findings are supported by the existing connections between meshes, spanning trees, and limited weight information. We further include additional simple mesh structures, the restricted alpha-shapes and spanning acycles, for added insight.
