The work addresses the group-isomorphism issue related to the algebraic transfer homomorphism for $(\mathscr A)_{\mathrm{Tr}}^s$.  The work also extends ideas to show that $\mathrm{Tr}^s$ generates an isomorphism of Ext-groups from $H^{\mathrm{s}}(\mathscr A_s)$ to $H^{\mathrm{s}}(\mathscr A, (\mathscr A

A far ultraviolet spectral range observational capability is being developed for the Daniel K. Inoue Space Station, an orbiting observatory located at a 500 km altitude with constant sunlight access. By utilizing a hydrogen absorption filter and a sparsely filled cryogenic calorimeter detector within a Schwarzschild telescope configuration, this instrument aims to provide accurate spectral measurements across the 120-200 nm spectrum. Cryogenic detector technology, particularly in charge extraction and charge collection layers, is being explored to enhance low signal detection efficiency and minimize thermal noise in spectrometry applications. By optimizing the cryogenic detector's properties and implementing novel extraction techniques, this instrument aims to achieve high signal processing accuracy and noise minimization, thus offering 1% precision spectral measurements. Initially, prototype assessments, including laboratory tests of the cryogenic detector, are being conducted. Subsequent experiments will involve on-site observations at various locations, later complemented by continuous laboratory testing for optimal instrument performance.

We investigate a type of system known as Graph Symmetric Systems, for controllability and observability properties in a distributed optimal control framework. This system is connected to a group of decentralized controllers based on distributed robust LQR design, which relates to previous studies on optimal barrier strategy by Carvalho et al. in 2018. By utilizing a new approach through Lyapunov kernel spectra, we show that optimal control strategies can be distributed and effective, even without system information. Furthermore, we develop a graphical condition that determines whether a optimal control configuration can be applied locally, and use this condition to analyze the relationship between controllability and connectivity within the system. Through this new approach, we identify system properties that enable distributed optimal control, even in systems with non-minimal realization.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications enhance the image's retrievability, with backproped versions of high-confidence images yielding a significant 42% increase in retrieval accuracy. Furthermore, active indexing significantly improves the neural embeddings' discriminability, increasing average pairwise similarity distance to 12. The improved embeddings result in a substantial 71% reduction in nearest-neighbor queries without additional computational cost.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian channels with an adversary, as long as the receiver's channel capacity
exceeds the equivalent channel capacity with the adversary neutralized. Furthermore,
we investigate the optimal input strategies for both the sender and receiver, as
well as any collaborating parties, to maximize the authentication reliability.
In this analysis, optimal input strategies are defined by seeking minimal
probability of incorrect authentication outcomes, and are found to involve a
form of partial cooperation between the sender and receiver under specified
conditions. In cases where such cooperation is prohibited, our results show that
the sender can still optimize authentication reliability by incorporating the
adversary's channel capacity in the sender's encoding process. Building upon this
foundation, we explore an extension of this concept in the context of multi-user
Gaussian channels with an adversary, and confirm that physical layer-based
authentication is achievable in the most challenging scenario, even in the presence
of simultaneous transmission from multiple users and the adversary. In this
extension, we investigate the optimal input strategies for both the sender and
receiving users, as well as any collaborating parties, to maximize the overall
authentication reliability. Once again, these optimal input strategies are found
to involve a form of partial cooperation between relevant entities. In cases where
such cooperation is prohibited, our results show that the sender can still achieve
optimal authentication reliability by incorporating the adversary's channel
capacity in the sender's encoding process.

Reevaluating the "dispersionless transport regime" of Brownian particles in inclined periodic potentials, we found that after entering a running state under the influence of a constant force, these particles display typical diffusive behavior without experiencing unique transient dynamics as previously hypothesized. The flat section in the dispersion evolution graph can be entirely attributed to the particles' wide spatial distribution resulting from an earlier stage of superdiffusion. Using a velocity space model with a 2-well potential, we thoroughly characterized the distribution function's progression during the superdiffusive and transitional phases to normal diffusion. The calculated exponent for superdiffusion was found to be 3. Additionally, our simulation to demonstrate transport without enhancement, where particles remain in the "running state" yet fail to reach the target, supports the theory that enhanced transport relies on the temporarily flat phase.

This paper presents an adaptable forecasting technique that builds upon an established model for forecasting Macroeconomic Variables, originally developed by Scotti (2012) in the context of real GDP growth. Extending the original approach, this research creates a framework capable of identifying multifaceted relationships between economic variables and their respective responses to fiscal stimuli. Initial results indicate a complex connection between financial markets and economic outcomes, including distinct reactions to contractionary and expansionary fiscal shocks under different economic circumstances. Conversely, the response to monetary stimuli reveals no significant variations in conditions. Subsequent to identifying these dynamic interactions, this study develops a forecasting method that enables the identification of underlying causes and effects, allowing for a unified forecasting framework that considers these interconnected elements. Moreover, this research establishes a clear distinction between variables that are directly observable and those that remain hidden, or latent. Latent Dirichlette Allocation, a topic modeling method, is employed in conjunction with Bayesian techniques to effectively utilize information from incompletely specified variables, while maintaining accurate data on specified variables and their normal distribution. Through an extensive analysis using data from the S&P dataset, this research confirms the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. Notably, this study's forecasting method achieves improvements over key benchmarks, or benchmark methods.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau level.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by addressing the class imbalance issue. Most FG-NET methods focus on refining output distributions by employing plausible world knowledge. However, balancing different class probabilities in FG-NET remains unaddressed. In response, we propose the HGC, a novel approach to tackle the class imbalance issue by modeling entity types within hyperbolic space, which naturally allows certain entity types to be closer to each other. By representing labels as points in hyperbolic space, the likelihood of rare labels is increased, improving their output distributions. Through experiments on benchmark datasets, the HGC approach achieves notable performance improvements, with an average increase in F1-score of 4.35% compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by a specific condition involving functions that are analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, with normalization where $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$.

This research introduces a new load balancing approach called Prepartition, which effectively reduces hotspots in cloud data centers by proactively distributing workloads among virtual machines and physical servers through predictive and real-time migration. Prepartition utilizes past workload trends and predictive models to partition virtual machines before their arrival, minimizing unpredictability and server overload. A secondary load balancing mechanism adjusts to immediate server demands and workload fluctuations. To account for uncertainty, probabilistic discrete event simulation is employed to evaluate performance. Extensive experimentation demonstrates that Prepartition outperforms adaptive load balancing with reactive migration, while also providing more accurate performance expectations.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic, or network conditions, beyond the control of agents, can impact game dynamics. Typically, researchers update game strategies based on outcomes but sometimes overlook the effect of chance events. Our study on rival cars navigating a highway reveals that, when these unexpected events occur infrequently, they can push the game towards unstable equilibrium where no stable state exists. On the other hand, when these events happen consistently, the system tends towards stable equilibrium where it reaches a stable state. A mathematical formula has been developed which indicates the frequency of these chance events directly affects the stability of the game, implying that regular occurrence of these events tends to stabilize it while infrequent occurrence tends to destabilize it.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two intricate optimization problems. The derived limits prove to be sufficient, leading us to introduce an optimization technique, enabling dimensionality reduction that lets users choose between bias minimization and increased estimation precision. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through controlled experiments.

Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, they may not be effective against covert attacks that bypass detection during prolonged operations. We present a statistical model to estimate the probability of a system being compromised by covert attacks, measurable in real-time with only system performance data available. This model's output can inform system operators about the risk level. Our approach relies on the hidden Markov model and requires training on time-series data of system performance, including instances of known attacks. In this study, we demonstrate its applicability using simulated data of physical systems and industrial motors. Our results indicate that this model generally identifies when a system is under attack and distinguishes it from normal operation, stochastic fluctuations, and transient phenomena.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger training sets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarization for lesser-known Indian languages is hindered by complex syntax and differences in meaning. A proposed model called BERT-IEC is offered as a solution, built upon a unique dataset (Hindi-IEC) that was created by pairing documents with their contracted forms to guide an editorating model towards optimal results. Furthermore, a diverse range of perspectives was incorporated into a dataset through crowdsourced editing of samples by non-experts as well as trained professionals, ensuring a diverse range of meanings and contexts that can be drawn upon during training. External evaluation of this approach has also been applied using a variety of automatic and human evaluation techniques. Results from these assessments have shown BERT-IEC to significantly surpass current best practices in summarization for Hindi, with similar potential to make a similar impact for other Indian languages as well.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We calculate the injective dimension of a quotient category formed by modules over an independent S-ring of type A, with respect to a specified subcategory consisting of modules having trivial interactions with codivisorial modules.

The objective of this research was to identify and characterise potential substellar companions associated with five rapidly accelerating stars using data derived from Gaia EDR3 and previous studies. These targets include HIP 1481, HIP 20321, HIP 53512, HIP 88399, and HIP 110590. For the purposes of this investigation, the criteria for selecting targets focused on rapid acceleration rates, as measured by Spitzer, and limited luminosities. What distinguishes this study from similar research is its adoption of statistical models that incorporate correlated data fluctuations to analyse light curve modulations. Using these approaches, predicted companion mass ranges spaned from 0.5 \m_J for HIP 1481 to 3 \m_J for HIP 88399. Ultimately, secure detections from photometric data proved elusive in this study, with the primary reason attributed to photometric limitations. Future studies may successfully detect companions of 0.1 \m_J in magnitude, provided that the host star brightness in the K2 regime does not exceed 5 \mag. Building upon this, research into other stars exhibiting similar effects may lead to a broader understanding of this phenomenon.

Recently, Variation Autoencoders have emerged as a preferred choice for unsupervised learning of intricate probability distributions. Compared to traditional autoencoders, VAEs exhibit enhanced reconstructive capabilities, making more accurate approximations possible even in the presence of noise, as opposed to Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. By utilizing a hierarchical series of probabilistic layers, VAEs formulate a generative process that involves generating a latent variable vector. However, optimizing this process is challenging due to its inherent imprecision, necessitating a trade-off between achieving better reconstructive results and generating more realistic samples. In an effort to strike the perfect balance, researchers continuously refine VAEs by incorporating various innovations. This paper undertakes a thorough examination of the trade-off between the quality of the reconstructive model and the diversity of the sample distribution in different Variational Autoencoder models.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by IoT, yet it also invites cyber threats that necessitate robust and cost-effective security measures. This research contributes to filling this need by designing an affordable, network security system utilizing a private blockchain and a location tracking technique based on wireless signal strength. Our investigation highlights the benefits of private blockchains and optimizes the location tracking accuracy by testing its performance with various wireless networks. The results demonstrate that integrating a private blockchain with Wi-Fi technology achieves the best results for our proposed system.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, which facilitated the design of a deep autoencoder. This autoencoder simultaneously compresses and separately reconstructs L-values using a weighted loss function prioritizing accurate reconstruction of lower-magnitude inputs. The proposed method was demonstrated to rival the performance of state-of-the-art maximum mutual information quantization schemes while requiring reduced memory. Specifically, it was shown that this method could decrease the memory footprint by up to two while maintaining less than 0.1 dB in performance loss in comparison to the optimal top-bit assignment.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-ALL and AL-PUB, where individual characters are closely cropped from these images. The application of ensemble modeling to datasets of this nature can aid in identifying and quantifying the reliability of images with uncertain labels. This can be achieved by incorporating the use of ensemble modeling with novel methods like knowledge distillation, which aims to refine the distribution of class probabilities, as well as selective training, which involves discarding uncertain data during the training process. Notably, ensemble modeling approach yields an exceptional level of precision with a macro-averaged AUC-PR of 97% for the case of individual characters on the AL-ALL dataset. The proposed methodology is subsequently expanded to employ selective training, which results in a further enhancement of the model's precision with a decreased ratio of uncertain data points, from 27.91% to 8.35%.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables. This result is pivotal in establishing uniform bounds on H\"older and Holder-Brascamp-Lieb norms of invariant Gibbs measures. Our approach is explicit and relies on an iterative method to construct the inverse of the transfer operator, which is based on a finite {\it Markov partition} cover of the underlying phase space. For nonuniformly expanding dynamics, we further require a {\it hyperbolic structure} for this construction to work. When the phase space is compact and the transfer operators are of weak contraction type, we can extend our result to partially expanding semiflows, which include, for instance, semiflows on noncompact manifolds with uniformly expanding vector fields along compact submanifolds. Additionally, we show the exponential decay in Brascamp-Lieb norms of invariant Gibbs measures for semiflows with uniformly expanding dynamics.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols a set number of times. The best, or smallest, such matrices are known as optimal, or optimal covering arrays. Covering arrays have various applications and their optimal versions have been the subject of much study. Researchers have developed a method to create optimal covering arrays of any size and symbol combination, given a specific set of constraints. The method utilizes a pre-existing optimal covering array, of the same size and symbol combination, but with one added constraint. This allows them to generate optimal covering arrays of any size and symbol combination, given just two constraints: the number of symbols and a further constraint, of the sizes of the sub-matrices. This type of optimal covering array is known as universally optimal. The researchers were able to show that, given the two constraints, it's possible to generate optimal covering arrays of any size and symbol combination, by using a well-known pre-existing optimal covering array, of the same size and symbol combination, but with one added constraint.

This paper examines a unique category of nonlocal games, denoted by $\mathcal{CHM}$, rooted in local transformations of noisy maximally entangled states. Initially, it is demonstrated that approximately exact quantum correlation protocols are inherent to games in this class, encompassing an expanded version of the game Chilean Poker, in addition to an optimized version of Five-Element Game. Subsequently, the investigation delves into rigorous standards for assessing the approximate precision of games within $\mathcal{CHM}$ and establishes two important criteria for such games to achieve optimal standards of precision. Ultimately, the analysis provides a framework for comparable analysis within more complex game classes.

This study partially replicates the work by Soltani et al. who introduced EvoCrash, a tool capable of replicating Java software failures via stack traces. It leverages a guided genetic algorithm to create reliable JUnit test cases. We examine EvoCrash's effectiveness alongside three existing methods, including STAR, JCHARMING, and MuCrash, initially exploring its potential to generate failure-inducing test cases. We discover that EvoCrash and its predecessor JCHARMING experienced the highest success rate in recreating crashes, however, both are surpassed by other methods when it comes to overall test case efficiency and efficiency in mimicking real user behavior. MuCrash, the system we initially aimed to improve upon, still demonstrates the highest effectiveness in our experiments. We suggest EvoCrash be modified to integrate the star-coverage algorithm and to optimize test case efficiency. Note that this study focused on software crashes and did not involve sensitive data such as user interactions.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity.

Photons are valuable tools used to explore the intense medium produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Recent research includes precise calculations of the influence of viscosity on photon emission in these collisions, taking place at RHIC and LHC. Thermal photons exhibit specific patterns of movement within the collision medium, influenced by the viscosity of this system. Viscosity notably diminishes the movement patterns of thermal photons compared to findings using an ideal model. However, when considering real-world conditions, other factors significantly impact photon emission, including movement patterns of particles and the breaking of charged particles. By distinguishing and separate the effects of viscosity and non-ideal flow, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the unique characteristics of the collision medium. Furthermore, movement patterns of particles can be related to specific properties of the collision medium, making its study highly relevant.

Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries, focusing on group theoretical methods for triangular and kagome lattices. These regular magnetic orders hold significance as potential ground states for various spin models, making them prime candidates for study. By adhering to a framework developed by Messio et al., we extended their initial approach to incorporate specific subgroupings of the p6m symmetry group, such as p6, p3, p3m1, and p31m. For kagome and triangular lattices fitting these groupings, we have identified all corresponding regular magnetic orders. Calculations were then performed to determine the energy and spin structure factors for each state examined.

Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which requires conservative estimations. In contrast, other approaches like the adapts BH method offer better performance, but their efficiency relies heavily on the covariance matrix, which can be difficult to calculate or inaccurate. In response to these challenges, we introduce a novel statistical algorithm that leverages a machine learning model to create "skeletonized" covariance matrices, which are then used by the adapts BH method to enhance the detection power of ATE by up to 50% or reduce the computational time. Our results demonstrate that the adaptive SBC method outperforms existing alternatives, with the full implementation offering better results than the relaxed variants.

The foundational parameters of inflation, particularly the slow-roll parameters, are crucial in modern cosmology as they dictate a fundamental aspect of the universe's model. A pressing question arises: What is the minimum number of distinct slow-roll parameters necessary to predict observable features in the cosmic microwave background accurately? To address this, we investigated whether one parameter could suffice, analyzing how fluctuations in the universal inflaton field's spatial curvature could be generated by random fluctuations in the coherent volume of the inflaton. Our predictions show that the spectral characteristics of these fluctuations can be described by a single parameter as long as the inflation lasts long enough. A corresponding long-lasting model of inflation was created that produces identical spectral patterns with today's observations, providing a framework that could be tested using future missions focused on measuring the cosmic microwave background.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass which deviates from the Standard Model's prediction by 7$\sigma$. The FNAL muon magnetic moment measurement also displays a $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy. In an effort to resolve the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2), we have investigated the type-X two Higgs doublet model. Our analysis focused on the type-X 2HDM's parameter space for $m_A < m_h$, where both the W boson and muon magnetic moment exhibit enhanced mass. Our results show that the type-X 2HDM can account for the $7\sigma$ deviation in the W boson mass and the $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy in the muon magnetic moment.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software system users, presenting the difficulty of choosing suitable 
search terms for concept location during maintenance activities. A proposed technique 
QUICKAR leverages the knowledge gathered from the crowd-sourced platform, Stack 
Overflow, to provide reformulated query suggestions based on the relevance of search 
terms. The relevance is established by comparing adjacent word patterns extracted from 
relevant programming questions on Stack Overflow. Preliminary experiments demonstrate 
the efficacy of this approach, highlighting its potential applications for other 
crowd-sourced data sets.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better track changes in a speaker's unique characteristics during an interaction, this study uses multivariate linear predictive coding to analyze acoustic features from speech recordings. Analyzing a dataset of conversations between strangers, this research investigates the degree to which individual differences in a speaker's voice, specifically their unique acoustic features, remain stable or change based on the level of conversational adaptation observed. The results reveal that when two individuals show significant interaction adaptation, the variation in their unique acoustic features decreases, while the primary features associated with each speaker's distinctive voice show varying degrees of stability or change.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (RCSED2). This comprehensive
catalog encompasses a vast collection of galaxy spectral and imaging data from
the second generation of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-II). Our image and
spectral visualization tools are designed to seamlessly integrate with other data
sources, including the RCSED2 catalog, and provide easy access to web-based
platforms like Jupyter Notebooks and Zen. This enables researchers to create dynamic
visualizations that can be directly linked to the RCSED2 catalog, making it
convenient to explore and download associated data.

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method, called SSCAP, that identifies likely temporal segments across a variety of videos without the need for explicit annotations. SSCAP utilizes self-supervised learning techniques to derive distinct visual features from each video frame and a novel action representation based on these features. Subsequently, we propose a novel method for partitioning temporal segments according to their internal consistency and global co-occurrence frequency. The effectiveness of SSCAP is demonstrated through its superior performance on HMDB51, UCF101, Sports1M, Kinetics, and YTB Action Recognition benchmarks under unsupervised and semi-supervised settings, even outperforming several leading unsupervised baselines and semi-supervised baselines with less information. The SSCAP method is accessible via the repository https://github.com/whd-750/SSCAP.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, and compute their masses, decay constants, and production rates through QCD sum rules. Utilizing current algebra, we then determine their relative production rates in $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. The $\bar D^{*} \Sigma_c$ and $D^{*} \Sigma_c^*$ molecular states are found to have shorter formation times compared to $D \Sigma_c^*$, enabling their survival in hadronic environments. The study further examines their decay properties and properties of mixed molecular states, and specifies criteria for identifying these molecular states through QCD sum rules.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student can easily create manually. As a result, students are not given the opportunity to apply advanced testing techniques, such as fault-based testing, which is both beneficial and essential in teaching students the concepts of testing. To address this issue, we present TBudget, an open-source testing learning tool designed to make testing learning a manageable task for both instructors and students by offering an easy-to-use framework for teaching eight fundamental testing concepts. The framework achieves this by providing a budget-friendly system for writing test cases that not only accurately simulates professional tool coverage but also enables students to apply more sophisticated testing techniques. The eight testing concepts taught by TBudget are configurable and customizable, allowing instructors to tailor the tool to suit their particular testing approach. By utilizing TBudget, students can apply more sophisticated testing techniques, such as fault-based testing, which is reflected in their score. To determine the effectiveness of TBudget, we conducted an experiment in which undergraduate students used the tool for an empirical study and evaluated its costs and benefits in relation to existing testing educational tools. The results showed that TBudget excelled above the average score of students using the traditional testing educational tool, TestingTeacher, and demonstrated a notable increase in its score. Additionally, we found that TBudget facilitated more sophisticated testing techniques, such as fault-based testing, which is particularly crucial in teaching students the concepts of testing.

Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. This approach involves a semi-supervised learning technique that iteratively utilizes entropy minimization and augmented label propagation for intra-domain and inter-domain alignments. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements of up to 19.9% compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in semi-supervised adaptation tasks.

A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick water reflector, utilizing a fuel mixture composed of fission gases, uranium-233, and fission products. A sophisticated Monte Carlo simulation methodology evaluates the performance of the system, incorporating thermodynamic analysis. It's noteworthy that the space nuclear power system must be robust enough to withstand launch conditions, including vibrations from rockets, and variations in radiation levels, (which can cause) localized heating of the reactor. Various parameters such as uranium-233 fuel loading, fission gas distribution, and reactor radius are analyzed to optimize system performance. A detailed time-dependent evaluation of the system, taking into account the effects of natural fission, is conducted, and it's found that the vaporization of the fuel mixture causes the reactor to operate at a steady state, defined by an optimized fuel-to-mass ratio.
